item.title: No. 3: Where does Staphylococcus aureus hide on a dairy goat farm?
item.description: S. aureus was found on 27 of 29 Dutch dairy goat farms, in goats, on workers' hands and in the environment. Airborne dust was where it was detected most often, and strains circulated mainly within each farm.
item.content:encoded:
The paper: Adetunji MFM, Pals MAM, Libera K, Kampfraath AA, Koop G, Vrieling M, Smit LAM (2026). A cross-sectional study of Staphylococcus aureus reservoirs in dairy goats, their environment and farm workers. One Health. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.onehlt.2026.101624

What did they ask?

Staphylococcus aureus is one of the important causes of mastitis in dairy goats, both clinical and subclinical. It lowers milk yield and quality, harms animal welfare and costs money. It is also a bacterium that colonises and infects people.

It is known to live in goats' noses and on their skin, but little was known about where else it is found on a farm and how it moves from one place to another. The authors, from Utrecht University and Wageningen (the Netherlands), set out to find out by looking at animals, people and the environment at the same time, an approach known as One Health.

What did they do?

Between February and May 2025 they visited 29 dairy goat farms across the country, with an average of about 1,100 goats in milk. They took 329 samples of four kinds:

  • the noses of 5 goats per farm (145 samples),
  • the hands of 1 to 4 workers or residents per farm (80 samples),
  • milking parlour teat cups, inside and outside (54 samples),
  • and airborne dust, collected with electrostatic dust collectors hung for about 5–7 days above the barn and above the milking parlour (50 samples).

They cultured the samples, identified the bacterium and sequenced the whole genome of the isolates. Sequencing shows whether bacteria from different places are the same strain.

What did they find?

It is on almost every farm. S. aureus was found on 27 of the 29 farms, and about 27% of all samples were positive. Within farms, the share of positive samples ranged from 0% to 58%.

Airborne dust was the reservoir with the most positives. More than half of the dust samples, from both the barn and the milking parlour, carried the bacterium. That is significantly more than goats' noses, hands or teat cups. Hands and teat cups were positive least often.

The same strains in goats, people and the environment. Sequencing showed that the dominant strain was ST133, the most typical of small ruminants (77% of isolates), followed by ST398 (10%). Isolates from noses, hands, teat cups and dust on the same farm were usually very closely related. Between farms, by contrast, they were rarely shared: of the 14 genetic clusters found, 10 occurred on a single farm.

Contact with goats and exposure. People who neither entered the barns nor handled the animals did not carry the bacterium on their hands. Most participants did not wear gloves.

Why does it matter?

The practical message is that farmers should assume S. aureus is present on the farm, even when there are no visible clinical cases. Subclinical mastitis is hard to detect and the bacterium can circulate unnoticed.

The study also suggests that mastitis control is not only about treating goats: the environment matters. Dust could be a transmission route between animals and to people. The authors therefore recommend strengthening hygiene, environmental management and milking routines, and studying less dusty bedding and better ventilation.

That strains circulate mainly within each farm is also good news: measures taken on each farm can make a difference.

Limitations

  • Volunteer farms. The farms that took part had signed up because they were interested in udder health, so they may not represent the whole sector.
  • Samples not comparable over time. Dust was collected over 5–7 days, while nose, hand and teat-cup swabs capture a single moment. This favours more positives in dust.
  • The statistics did not account for the farm. Samples from all farms were pooled without considering that samples from the same farm resemble each other, as the authors themselves point out.
  • Only hands were sampled in people, not noses, which are the most common human reservoir. Presence in workers is probably underestimated.
  • Culture can miss the bacterium when other species overgrow the plate, so the method's sensitivity is uncertain.
  • It is a cross-sectional study: it shows where the bacterium is at one point in time, but does not prove how it is transmitted.

item.title: No. 2: Paratuberculosis in goats: does the vaccination route matter for the gut's immune response?
item.description: Ten months after infection, the immune response in the goats' gut depended mainly on how severe the lesions were, not on whether the animals had been vaccinated orally, intradermally or subcutaneously.
item.content:encoded:
The paper: Criado M, Silva M, Mendívil P, Zapico D, Pérez-Rojo V, Benavides J, Espinosa J, Elguezabal N, Gutiérrez-Expósito D (2026). Jejunal mucosal immune response in goats ten months after Mycobacterium avium subsp. paratuberculosis challenge is primarily determined by lesion severity rather than vaccination route. Veterinary Quarterly. https://doi.org/10.1080/01652176.2026.2707278

What did they ask?

Paratuberculosis is a chronic enteritis caused by Mycobacterium avium subsp. paratuberculosis (Map). It progresses slowly, reduces production and increases mortality in herds. Vaccination is the best tool to control clinical disease, but current vaccines, given subcutaneously, have drawbacks: protection is incomplete, they leave a granuloma at the injection site and they interfere with bovine tuberculosis diagnosis.

In an earlier study, the same group from the University of León and CSIC (Spain) compared two experimental vaccines in goats, one oral and one intradermal, with the commercial subcutaneous vaccine (Gudair®). The commercial vaccine protected best, but the oral vaccine reduced lesion severity and the intradermal one reduced bacterial load.

This time they wanted to know what happens where the battle is actually fought: the gut mucosa. Does each vaccination route leave a different mark on the local immune response?

What did they do?

They worked with 28 one-month-old goat kids from the earlier study:

  • 6 received the oral vaccine,
  • 6 the intradermal vaccine,
  • 6 the commercial subcutaneous vaccine,
  • and 10 were left unvaccinated.

One month later, half of each vaccinated group (3 animals) and 7 of the unvaccinated kids were experimentally infected with Map. Ten months after infection, all animals were euthanised and a Peyer's patch from the distal jejunum was analysed, the area with the most lesions and bacteria.

They counted macrophages and their two main types (M1, more inflammatory, and M2, more regulatory), γδ T cells and IgA-producing plasma cells. They also analysed the expression of several cytokines, the response of gut cells when re-exposed to the antigen, and Map-specific IgA in the intestinal contents. Lesions were classed as focal (small, localised granulomas), multifocal or diffuse (granulomas spread throughout the mucosa).

What did they find?

The vaccination route mattered little. In uninfected animals, the gut response was very similar with any vaccine or none. The only exception was IL-17A, an inflammatory cytokine, which was increased in all vaccinated groups.

Lesion severity mattered most. When animals were grouped by lesion type, clear differences emerged:

  • Focal lesions: the profile pointed to a Th1-type response, the kind linked to controlling infection. M1 macrophages and γδ T cells clustered around the granulomas, and the local interferon-gamma response was higher.
  • Diffuse lesions: there were many more macrophages, especially of the M2 type, which is considered more permissive to the bacterium. When stimulated, the cells produced more IL-4, consistent with a response starting to shift towards the Th2 type, which is less effective against mycobacteria.

Gut IgA tracked the infection. Map-specific IgA in the jejunal contents was higher in infected animals. It correlated with bacterial load in faeces (ρ = 0.76) and in the Peyer's patch (ρ = 0.69), and with serum IgG (ρ = 0.68). In animals with focal lesions, by contrast, it was barely different from uninfected animals.

The oral vaccine stood apart. Kids vaccinated orally and then infected expressed less IL-1β and IL-17A and had fewer macrophages. The authors suggest this could explain why their lesions were milder despite a high bacterial load. But they caution that this does not mean good infection control: the oral vaccine seems to decouple inflammation from bacterial burden without clearing the bacterium.

Why does it matter?

Finding paratuberculosis vaccines that do not interfere with tuberculosis diagnosis or leave granulomas is a priority. Oral and intradermal routes are candidates, but what they do in the ruminant gut had hardly been studied.

This work carries two messages. First, in the long run the gut response is shaped mainly by how infection progresses in each animal, more than by the vaccine received. So when comparing vaccines in experimental studies, it helps to group animals by lesion type. Second, fewer lesions do not always mean fewer bacteria, as the oral vaccine shows.

In addition, specific IgA in the jejunal contents could serve, under experimental conditions, as a marker of disease progression or vaccine efficacy.

Limitations

  • Very few animals per group. Only 3 vaccinated and infected kids per route, with high variability between individuals. The authors acknowledge this limits conclusions about each vaccine's effect.
  • A single sampling time. Everything was measured ten months after infection. The vaccine's initial effect may have faded by then, and how the response evolved over time is unknown.
  • Experimental infection. Conditions do not fully reproduce natural infection in a herd.
  • One part of the gut. The study looked at the distal jejunal Peyer's patch, the most affected site in this model, but not other parts of the intestine.

item.title: No. 1: Can preservatives slow bacterial growth in stored goat colostrum?
item.description: Potassium sorbate and sodium benzoate held back bacterial growth in goat colostrum, both refrigerated and at room temperature. Sodium lactate barely helped. They are an extra safeguard, not a replacement for cooling and hygiene.
item.content:encoded:
The paper: Liang F, Capdevila Ospina K, Cameron AWN, DiGiacomo K, Zamuner F (2026). Evaluating the temperature-dependent effects of 3 preservative treatments on bacterial growth in raw goat colostrum. Journal of Dairy Science. https://doi.org/10.3168/jds.2026-28527

What did they ask?

Goat kids are born without antibodies: the goat placenta does not let them through, so all early immunity depends on colostrum. But raw colostrum can become contaminated with bacteria during storage. Those bacteria can make kids sick and may also interfere with immunoglobulin absorption in the gut.

Refrigeration, freezing or pasteurisation help, but they are not always practical on farm. Chemical preservatives for colostrum have been tested in cattle, but hardly at all in goats. The authors wanted to know whether three food-grade preservatives slow bacterial growth in goat colostrum, both refrigerated and at room temperature.

What did they do?

They collected fresh colostrum from about 27 does on two commercial farms in Victoria, Australia, keeping only good-quality colostrum (Brix of at least 20%), and pooled it into a single batch. They split it into four groups:

  • no preservative (control),
  • potassium sorbate at 0.5%,
  • sodium benzoate at 0.5%,
  • sodium lactate at 0.3%.

Samples were stored at 4 °C for one week (up to 168 hours) and at 25 °C for two days (up to 48 hours), mimicking the fridge and colostrum left out during collection or transport. At set times they counted coliforms, Escherichia coli and total bacteria, and measured pH.

What did they find?

Bacterial counts are on a log scale: a difference of 1 log means 10 times more bacteria, and 3 log means about 1,000 times more.

In the fridge (4 °C). All samples stayed stable for the first two days. By the end of the week, untreated colostrum had reached almost 7 log coliforms. With sorbate or benzoate, coliforms stayed close to the starting level (about 4 log), roughly 1,000 times fewer than the control. Total bacteria were also more than 1.3 log lower with these two preservatives. E. coli stayed low in every group, with or without preservative.

At room temperature (25 °C). Without preservative, bacteria took off: coliforms reached 6.7 log at 12 hours and total bacteria exceeded 9 log at 24 hours. Sorbate and benzoate made a difference as early as 6 hours, and at 12 hours coliforms were 2.4 to 2.9 log below the control. With them, E. coli stayed near or below the detection limit.

Sodium lactate did not work. At 0.3%, it followed almost the same course as the control at both temperatures.

Why does it matter?

The study supports a two-barrier approach. The first and main barrier is cold: temperature had the biggest influence on bacterial growth. The second would be sorbate or benzoate, most useful in two common farm situations: the first hours when colostrum sits at room temperature before it reaches the fridge, and when it is kept refrigerated for longer than planned.

The authors are clear: these preservatives reduce risk, but they do not replace good hygiene or the cold chain.

Limitations

  • A single batch of colostrum. Everything was done with one pooled sample from two farms, which in practice equals one biological replicate. The authors themselves regard the results as preliminary.
  • Immunoglobulins were not measured. We do not know whether the preservatives affect IgG in goat colostrum, or whether they improve immunity in the kids that drink it.
  • Little E. coli to begin with. With such low counts, it cannot be claimed that these preservatives work specifically against E. coli.
  • Laboratory conditions. They do not capture real differences in hygiene, equipment and contamination between farms.
